Write a program to print a square matrix spirally.

![A grid of numbers arranged in six rows and six columns, each cell containing a two-digit number, randomly distributed throughout the table. ](images/Figure_2.010.png)

Figure 2.10 Square matrix

If the given matrix is printed spirally, the output would be:

95 67 32 35 44 65 59 17 20 37 22 36 14 52 38 19 39 24 82 12 11 16 93 29 27 33 34 23 26 30 18 13 21 31 15 28

The following figure shows the indices of elements and the order in which they are printed:

![A grid showing pairs of numbers, some in the top left and some in the center right, with text groups below: (0.0 to 0.5), (1.5 to 5.0), (5.4 to 5.0), (4.0 to 1.0), etc. ](images/Figure_2.011.png)

Figure 2.11 Indices of elements and print order

//P15.java : Program to print a square matrix spirally.

class P15Demo

{

public static void main(String[] args)

{

int[][] arr =

{

{95,67,32,35,44,65},

{12,11,16,93,29,59},

{82,13,21,31,27,17},

{24,18,28,15,33,20},

{39,30,26,23,34,37},

{19,38,52,14,36,22}

};

int n = arr.length;

int i,j,start,end;

System.out.println(“The square matrix is :”);

for(i=0; i<n; i++)

{

for(j=0; j<n; j++)

System.out.printf(“%5d”,arr[i][j]);

System.out.println();

}

System.out.println(“\nPrinting the square matrix spirally :”);

for(start=0,end=n-1; start<=end; start++,end--)

{

for(i=start; i<=end; i++)

System.out.print(arr[start][i] + “ “);

for(i=start+1; i<=end; i++)

System.out.print(arr[i][end] + “ “);

for(i=end-1; i>=start; i--)

System.out.print(arr[end][i] + “ “);

for(i=end-1; i>=start+1; i--)

System.out.print(arr[i][start] + “ “);

}

System.out.println();

}//End of main()

}//End of class P15Demo

# Linked Lists

3

List is a collection of similar type of elements. There are two ways of maintaining a list in memory. The first way is to store the elements of the list in an array. However, arrays have some restrictions and disadvantages. The second way of maintaining a list in memory is through a linked list. Let us study what a linked list is, and after that, we will come to know how it overcomes the limitations of the array.

## 3.1 Single Linked List

A single linked list is made up of nodes where each node has two parts; the first one is the info part that contains the actual data of the list, and the second one is the link part that refers to the next node of the list, or we can say, it contains the reference to the next node.

![Diagram of a list node with two sections: INFO for actual data and LINK pointing to the next node, with arrows and labels explaining each part‚Äôs function. ](images/Figure_3.001.png)

Figure 3.1 Node of a single linked list

The beginning of the list is referred by a reference named start. This reference refers to the first node of the list. The link part of each node refers to the next node in the list, but the link part of the last node has no next node to refer to. Thus, it is made null. Hence, if we reach a node whose link part has null value, then we know that we are at the end of the list. Suppose we have a list of four integers 33, 44, 55, 66; let us see how we will represent it through a linked list.

![A flowchart starting at 350, branching to 33 (350), then to 44 (900), then to 55 (150), and finally to 66 (700). Each box contains a bold number with a value below it. ](images/Figure_3.002.png)

Figure 3.2 Single linked list

From figure 3.2, it is clear that the info part contains the integer values, and the link part refers to the next node. The reference start refers to the first node and the link part of last node is null (represented by shaded part in the figure).

If we observe the memory locations of the nodes, we find that the nodes are not necessarily located adjacent to each other in the memory. The following figure shows the position of nodes of the preceding list in memory:

![A timeline diagram with labeled intervals: 150, 350, 700, and 900\. Markers indicate points at 55 (700), 33 (900), 66 (mil), and 44 (150). An arrow labeled start 350 points to the 350 interval. ](images/Figure_3.003.png)

Figure 3.3 Single linked list in memory

We can see that the nodes are scattered around in memory, although they are connected to each other through the link part, which also maintains their linear order. Now, let us see the picture of memory if the same list of integers is implemented through an array:

![A horizontal number line with tick marks at 33, 44, 55, and 66 on the top, and 330, 364, 398, and 362 on the bottom. Dotted lines extend to the left and right of the ticks. ](images/Figure_3.004.png)

Figure 3.4 List in array

Here, the elements are stored in consecutive memory locations in the same order as they appear in the list. So, the array is a sequential representation of the list, while the linked list is a linked representation of the list. In a linked list, nodes are not stored contiguously as in an array, but they are linked through references (links), and we can use these links to move through the list.

Now, let us see how we can represent a node of a single linked list in Java. We will take a self-referential class for this purpose. Recall that a self-referential class is a class that contains a data member reference to an object of the same class type. The general form of a node of linked list is:

class Node

{

public data member1;

public data member2;

……………………………………

……………………………………

public Node link; //Reference to next node

}

Let us see some examples of nodes:

![Three class Node code examples with diagrams: one holds an int value, another stores name, code, salary, and the third has a Student object; each includes a link field pointing to the next node. ](images/Figure_3.005.png)

Figure 3.5 Node examples

In this chapter, we will perform all operations on linked lists that contain only an integer value in the info part of their nodes. Here is the class Node:

class Node

{

public int info;

public Node link;

public Node(int data)

{

info = data;

link = null;

}

}//End of class Node

In the constructor of Node, data members info and link are initialized during the creation of the node. A node will be created in this way:

Node temp = new Node(10);

In an array, we could perform all the operations using the array name and index. In the case of the linked list, we will perform all the operations with the help of the reference start of type Node because it is the only source through which we can access our linked list. It refers to the first node of the list. The list will be considered empty if the reference start contains null value. So, our first job is to declare the reference start and initialize it to null. This will be in class SingleLinkedList which will have start as data member and will have methods for operations of single linked list. Here is the class SingleLinkedList:

class SingleLinkedList

{

private Node start;

//Methods

..........

..........

}//End of class SingleLinkedList

The data member start is initialized to null in constructor, during the creation of the SingleLinkedList object. The start will refer to the first node of list once nodes of linked lists are created. The public methods provides the operations of the linked list and they use private method and data member start. The SingleLinkedList object is created in this way:

SingleLinkedList listObj = new SingleLinkedList();

This is the constructor of class SingleLinkedList:

public SingleLinkedList()

{

start = null;

}//End of SingleLinkedList()

We will discuss the following operations on a single linked list.

*   Traversal of a linked list
*   Searching an element
*   Insertion of an element
*   Deletion of an element
*   Creation of a linked list
*   Reversal of a linked list

The main() method is available in another class SingleLinkedListDemo and given next. The code of methods of class SingleLinkedList are given with the explanation of operations.

//SingleLinkedList.java : Program of Single linked list.

class SingleLinkedListDemo

{

public static void main(String[] args)

{

In the main() method, we are creating the SingleLinkedList object. So, the constructor of SingleLinkedList is invoked and start is initialized with null. The SingleLinkedList object is used to invoke the insertion methods for creating the initial list of nodes. The reference start will be referring to the first node of list.

The data member Node reference start is available to all the methods. So, by using start, methods can access the linked list.

There will be many operations which will first need to check if the list is empty or not. That can be easily done by checking the value of start as start will have value null if there is no node in the list. The following method isEmpty() will return the appropriate value:

public boolean isEmpty()

{

return (start == null);

}//End of isEmpty()

### 3.1.1 Traversing a Single Linked List

Traversal means visiting each node, starting from the first node until reaching the last node. For this, we will take a Node reference p, which will refer to the node that is currently being visited. Initially, we have to visit the first node so p is assigned the value of start.

p = start;

Now, p refers to the first node of the linked list. We can access the info part of the first node by writing p.info. Now we have to move the reference p forward so that it refers to the next node. This can be done by assigning the reference to the next node p.link to p as:

p = p.link;

Now, p refers to the next node. Similarly, we can visit each node of the linked list through this assignment until p has a null value, which is the link part value of the last element. So, the linked list can be traversed as:

while(p != null)

{

System.out.println(p.info);

p = p.link;

}

Let us take an example to understand how the assignment p = p.link makes the reference p move forward. From now onwards, we will not show the memory locations, we will show only the info part of the list in the figures:

![A flowchart showing a linked list with five nodes labeled A to E, containing values 11, 22, 33, 44, and 55, connected sequentially from left to right, starting from start. ](images/Figure_3.006.png)

Figure 3.6 Single linked list example

In figure 3.6, node A is the first node, so start refers to it; node E is the last node, so its link is null.

Initially, p refers to node A, p.info gives 11, and p.link refers to node B

After the statement p = p.link;

p refers to node B, p.info gives 22, and p.link refers to node C.

After the statement p = p.link;

p refers to node C, p.info gives 33, and p.link refers to node D.

After the statement p = p.link;

p refers to node D, p.info gives 44, and p.link refers to node E.

After the statement p = p.link;

p refers to node E, p.info gives 55, and p.link is null.

After the statement p = p.link;

p becomes null, i.e., we have reached the end of the list so we come out of the loop.

The following method display() displays the contents of the linked list:

public void display()

{

Node p;

if(!isEmpty())

{

p = start;

while(p != null)

{

System.out.println(p.info);

p = p.link;

}

}

else

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

}//End of display()

Do not think of using start for moving forward. If we use start = start.link, instead of p = p.link, then we will lose start and that is the only means of accessing our list.

The following member method size() returns the number of elements in the linked list.

public int size()

{

Node p;

int count = 0;

p = start;

while(p != null)

{

count++;

p = p.link;

}

return count;

}//End of size()

### 3.1.2 Searching in a Single Linked List

For searching an element, we traverse the linked list and while traversing, we compare the info part of each element with the given element to be searched. In the method given below, nodeData is the element which we want to find:

public int find(int nodeData)

{

Node p = start;

int position = 0;

while(p != null)

{

position++;

if(p.info == nodeData)

return position;

p = p.link;

}

return 0;

}//End of find()

### 3.1.3 Insertion in a Single Linked List

There can be four cases while inserting a node in a linked list:

*   Insertion at the beginning
*   Insertion in an empty list
*   Insertion at the end
*   Insertion in between the list nodes

To insert a node, we will initially create the Node object using the new operator. We will pass the data value while creating the node, so that it will be assigned to data member info in the constructor of Node.

Node temp = new Node(data);

The link part of the node will be assigned null value in Node constructor. In our explanation, we will refer to this new node as node T.

#### 3.1.3.1 Insertion at the Beginning of the List

We have to insert node T at the beginning of the list. Suppose, the first node of list is node P. Thus, the new node T should be inserted before it.

![Diagram showing insertion at the beginning of a linked list: before, start points to node P; after, new node T is inserted at the beginning, start points to T, and T points to P. ](images/Figure_3.007.png)

Figure 3.7 Insertion at the beginning of the list

(i) Link of node T should refer to node P, and we know that start refers to node P so we should write:

temp.link = start;

After this statement, link of node T will refer to node P.

(ii) We want to make node T the first node; hence, we should update start so that now, it refers to node T.

start = temp;

The order of the above two statements is important. First, we should make the link of T equal to start and after that only, we should update start. Let us see what happens if the order of these two statements is reversed.

start = temp;

start refers to temp and we lost the reference to node P.

temp.link = start;

Link of temp will refer to itself because start refers to temp. So, if we reverse the order, then the link of node T will refer to itself and we will be stuck in an infinite loop when the list is processed.

The following method insertAtBeginning() adds a node at the beginning of the list:

public void insertAtBeginning(int data)

{

Node temp;

temp = new Node(data);

if(!isEmpty())

temp.link = start;

start = temp;

}//End of insertAtBeginning()

#### 3.1.3.2 Insertion in an Empty List

![Diagram showing linked list insertion: Before insertion, start points to null. After insertion, start points to node T, and the link from T is null, making T the only node in the list. ](images/Figure_3.008.png)

Figure 3.8 Insertion in an empty list

When the list is empty, value of start will be null. The new node that we are adding will be the only node in the list. Since it is the first node, start should refer to this node, and it is also the last node. Thus, its link should be null. While creating the new node, we are already setting the link part with null in the Node constructor.

start = temp;

This case is taken care of in the previous case (3.1.3.1) where we are checking if list is not empty. Then only,

temp.link refers to next node.

#### 3.1.3.3 Insertion at the End of the List

We have to insert a new node T at the end of the list. Suppose the last node of list is node P. Then, node T should be inserted after node P:

![Diagram showing a linked list before and after inserting a new node. Before: list ends at Node P. After: Node T is added after Node P, making Node T the last node and Node Ps link points to Node T. ](images/Figure_3.009.png)

Figure 3.9 Insertion at the end of the list

Suppose we have a reference p referring to the node P. This is the statement that should be written for this insertion:

p.link = temp;

link part of temp is already assigned with null while creating the node temp.

So, in this case we should have a reference p referring to the last node of the list. The only information about the linked list that we have is the reference start. So, we will traverse the list till the end, to get the reference p referring to the last node and then do the insertion. This is how reference p refers to the last node:

p = start;

while(p.link != null)

p = p.link;

In traversal of list (3.1.1) our terminating condition was (p != null), because there we wanted the loop to terminate when p becomes null. Here, we want the loop to terminate when p is referring to the last node so the terminating condition is (p.link != null).

The following method insertAtEnd() inserts a node at the end of the list:

public void insertAtEnd(int data)

{

Node p, temp;

temp = new Node(data);

if(isEmpty())

start = temp;

else

{

p = start;

while(p.link != null)

p = p.link;

p.link = temp;

}

}//End of insertAtEnd()

#### 3.1.3.4 Insertion in Between the List Nodes

We have to insert a node T between nodes P and Q:

![Diagram showing insertion in a linked list: Before insertion, Node Q follows Node P. After insertion, Node T is added between P and Q, with P pointing to T and T pointing to Q. Start and end nodes are indicated. ](images/Figure_3.010.png)

Figure 3.10 Insertion in between the list nodes

Suppose we have two references p and q referring to nodes P and Q respectively. The two statements that should be written for insertion of node T are:

temp.link = q;

p.link = temp;

Before insertion, p.link refers to node Q, and so instead of reference q, we can write p.link. Now the two statements for insertion can be written as:

temp.link = p.link;

p.link = temp;

Note: The order of these two statements is important. If you write them in the reverse order, then you will lose your links. The reference p.link refers to node Q. Suppose we write the statement (p.link = temp;) first, then we will lose the reference to node Q; there is no way to reach node Q and our list is broken. So first, the link of node T should refer to node Q by writing (temp.link = p.link). Now we have reference to node Q, and we are free to change p.link.

Now we will see three cases of insertion in between the nodes:

*   Insertion after a node
*   Insertion before a node
*   Insertion at a given position

The two statements of insertion (temp.link = p.link; p.link = temp;) will be written in all three cases, but the way of finding the reference p will be different.

##### 3.1.3.4.1 Insertion After a Node

In this case, we are given a value from the list, and we have to insert the new node after the node that contains this value. Suppose the node P contains the given value, and node Q is its successor. We have to insert the new node T after node P, i.e., T is to be inserted between nodes P and Q. In the method below, data is the new value to be inserted and nodeData is the value contained in node P. For writing the two statements of insertion (temp.link = p.link; p.link = temp;), we need reference p to refer to the node that contains nodeData. The procedure is the same as we have seen in searching of an element in the linked list.

public void insertAfter(int data, int nodeData)

{

Node p, temp;

p = start;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

while(p != null)

{

if(p.info == nodeData)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = p.link;

p.link = temp;

break;

}

p = p.link;

}

if(p == null)

System.out.println(“Item “ + nodeData + “ is not in the list”);

}//End of else

}//End of insertAfter()

Let us see what happens if nodeData is present in the last node, and we have to insert after it. In this case, p refers to the last node, and its link is null, so temp.link is again assigned null, and we do not have any need for a special case of insertion at the end. This method will work correctly even if we insert it after the last node.

##### 3.1.3.4.2 Insertion Before a Node

In this case, we are given a value from the list, and we have to insert the new node before the node that contains this value. Let us suppose that node Q contains the given value, and node P is its predecessor. We have to insert the new node T before node Q, i.e., T is to be inserted between nodes P and Q. In the method given as follows, data is the new value to be inserted, and nodeData is the value contained in node Q. For writing the two statements of insertion (temp.link = p.link; p.link = temp;) we need reference p referring to the predecessor of the node that contains nodeData. Since nodeData is present in Q and we have to get a reference p referring to node P, here the condition for searching would be if(p.link.info == nodeData) and the terminating condition of the loop would be (p.link != null).

public void insertBefore(int data, int nodeData)

{

Node p, temp;

p = start;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else if(p.info == nodeData) //nodeData is in first node

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = p;

start = temp;

}

else

{

//Get the reference to predecessor of node containing nodeData

while(p.link != null)

{

if(p.link.info == nodeData)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = p.link;

p.link = temp;

break;

}

p = p.link;

}

if(p.link == null)

System.out.println(“Item “ + nodeData + “ is not in the List”);

}//End of else

}//End of insertBefore()

If the node is to be inserted before the first node, then that case has to be handled separately because we have to update start in this case. If the list is empty, start will be null and the term p.info (p initially refers to start) will create problems. As such, before checking the condition if(p.info == nodeData) we should check for empty list.

##### 3.1.3.4.3 Insertion at a Given Position

In this case, we have to insert the new node at a given position. The two insertion statements are same as in the previous cases (temp.link = p.link; p.link = temp;).

The way of getting reference p referring to the right node is different. If we have to insert at the first position, we will have to update start, so that case is handled separately.

public void insertAtPosition(int data, int position)

{

Node p, temp;

if(position == 1)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = start;

start = temp;

}

else

{

p = start;

int index = 1;

//Get the reference to (position-1)th node

while(p!=null && index < position-1)

{

p = p.link;

index++;

}

if(p!=null && position>0)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = p.link;

p.link = temp;

}

else

System.out.println(“Item cannot be inserted at position : “ + position);

}//End of else

}//End of insertAtPosition()

### 3.1.4 Creation of a Single Linked List

A list can be created using insertion operations. First time, we will have to insert into an empty list, and then we will keep inserting nodes at the end of the list or insert at the beginning of the list or using any other insertion operation.

//Create the List

SingleLinkedList list = new SingleLinkedList();

list.insertAtEnd(10);

list.insertAtEnd(20);

list.insertAtEnd(30);

list.insertAtEnd(40);

list.insertAtEnd(50);

### 3.1.5 Deletion in a Single Linked List

For deletion of any node, the references are rearranged so that this node is removed from the list. The removed node will be claimed by the garbage collector. There can be four cases while deleting an element from a linked list:

*   Deletion of first node
*   Deletion of the only node
*   Deletion in between the list
*   Deletion at the end

#### 3.1.5.1 Deletion of First Node

![Two diagrams show linked list node deletion. Before: start points to Node T, linked to Node P. After: start points to Node P; Node T is removed. Text explains node references before and after deletion. ](images/Figure_3.011.png)

Figure 3.11 Deletion of first node

The node to be deleted is the first node. Since start refers to the first node of the linked list, start.link will refer to the second node. After deletion of the first node, the second node (node P) would become the first one. Thus, start should refer to node P as:

start = start.link;

After this statement, start refers to node P, so now it is the first node of the list.

The method deleteAtBeginning() deletes the node at the beginning of the list.

public void deleteAtBeginning()

{

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

start = start.link;

}//End of deleteAtBeginning()

#### 3.1.5.2 Deletion of the Only Node

If there is only one node in the list and we have to delete it, then after deletion the list would become empty and start would have null value.

![Diagram showing linked list deletion. Before: start points to node T with a null link. After: start is set to null, indicating the list is empty. Text explains T is the only node before deletion. ](images/Figure_3.012.png)

Figure 3.12 Deletion of the only node

start = null;

Here, we can write start.link instead of null. So, this case reduces to the first one (3.1.5.1).

#### 3.1.5.3 Deletion in Between the List Nodes

![Diagram showing linked list node deletion. Before: start points to P (which links to T, then Q). After: P links to Q (skipping T), illustrating node removal. Nodes and links are labeled accordingly. ](images/Figure_3.013.png)

Figure 3.13 Deletion in between the list nodes

Suppose node T is to be deleted and we have references p and q which refers to nodes P and Q respectively. For deletion of node T, we will just link the predecessor of T (node P) to successor of T (node Q).

p.link = q;

The link of node T refers to node Q, so instead of q, we can write p.link.link in the above statement.

p.link = p.link.link;

Now we will see two cases of deletion in between the nodes:

*   Delete a node specified with value
*   Deletion of a node at a given position

The statement for deletion (p.link = p.link.link;) will be the same in both cases, but the way of finding the reference p will be different.

##### 3.1.5.3.1 Delete a Node Specified with Value

In this case, we have to find the node with specified value. The value is in node T and we need reference p referring to its predecessor which is node P, so our condition for searching will be if(p.link.info == nodeData). Here, nodeData is the value in node to be deleted.

The method deleteNode() deletes the node which has specified value.

public void deleteNode(int nodeData)

{

Node p;

p = start;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else if(p.info == nodeData) //Deletion of first node

{

start = p.link;

}

else //Deletion in between or at the end

{

while(p.link != null)

{

if(p.link.info == nodeData)

break;

p = p.link;

}

if(p.link == null)

System.out.println(nodeData + “ not found in list”);

else

{

p.link = p.link.link;

}

}//End of else

}//End of deleteNode()

The first node deletion is handled separately because after deletion, start has to be updated.

##### 3.1.5.3.2 Deletion of a Node at a Given Position

In this case, we have to delete the node at a given position. The deletion statement is same as in the previous case (p.link = p.link.link;).

The way of getting reference p referring to the right node is different. If we have to delete at the first position, then we will have to update start. Thus, that case is handled separately.

public void deleteAtPosition(int position)

{

Node p;

p = start;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else if(position == 1)

{

start = start.link;

}

else

{

int index = 1;

while(p.link!=null && index < position-1)

{

p = p.link;

index++;

}

if(p.link!=null && position>0)

{

p.link = p.link.link;

}

else

System.out.println(“Node cannot be deleted at position : “ + position);

}//End of else

}//End of deleteAtPosition()

#### 3.1.5.4 Deletion at the End of the List

![Diagram showing deletion of the last node in a linked list. Before deletion, node P points to node T. After deletion, node P is the last node, and its next link is null. ](images/Figure_3.014.png)

Figure 3.14 Deletion at the end of the list

If p is a reference to node P, then the node T can be deleted by writing the following statement:

p.link = null;

Since the link of node T is null, so in the above statement, instead of null, we can write p.link.link. Hence, we can write this statement as:

p.link = p.link.link;

So, we can see that this case is reduced to the previous case (3.1.5.3). Here we want the loop to terminate when p is referring to the predecessor of the last node.

public void deleteAtEnd()

{

Node p;

p = start;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else if(p.link == null)

start = p.link;

else

{

while(p.link.link != null)

p = p.link;

p.link = null;

}

}//End of deleteAtEnd()

The first and only node deletion is handled separately to update the start.

### 3.1.6 Copy Constructor

Here is the copy constructor of a single linked list:

public SingleLinkedList(SingleLinkedList list)

{

if(list.start == null)

start = null;

else

{

Node p1, p2;

p1 = list.start;

p2 = start = new Node(p1.info);

p1 = p1.link;

while(p1 != null)

{

p2.link = new Node(p1.info);

p2 = p2.link;

p1 = p1.link;

}

}

}//End of copy constructor

### 3.1.7 Reversing a Single Linked List

The following changes need to be done in a single linked list for reversing it:

1. The first node should become the last node of linked list.

2. Last node should become the first node of linked list, and now start should refer to it.

3. The link of 2nd node should refer to 1st node; link of 3rd node should refer to 2nd node and so on.

Let us take a single linked list and reverse it:

![A linked list diagram showing a start node pointing to Node A (5), then arrows to Node B (15), Node C (20), and Node D (25), with Node D‚Äôs box shaded. ](images/Figure_3.015.png)

Figure 3.15 Single linked list

(i) Node A is the first node so start refers to it.

(ii) Node D is the last node, so its link is null.

(iii) Link of A refers to B, link of B refers to C and link of C refers to D.

After reversing, the linked list would be:

![Flowchart with labeled boxes Node A (5), Node B (15), Node C (20), Node D (25) connected by arrows in sequence from start, with Node A containing a shaded area. ](images/Figure_3.016.png)

Figure 3.16 Reversed single linked list

(i) Node D is the first node so start refers to it.

(ii) Node A is the last node, so its link is null.

(iii) Link of D refers to C, link of C refers to B and link of B refers to A.

Now, let us see how we can do the reversal of a linked list. We will take three references prev, p and next. Initially, the reference p will refer to start and prev will be null. In each pass, first the link of p is assigned to next and after that the link of p is changed, so that it refers to its previous node. The references prev and p are moved forward. Here is the method reverse(), that reverses a linked list:

public void reverse()

{

Node prev, p, next;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

p = start;

prev = null;

while(p != null)

{

next = p.link;

p.link = prev;

prev = p;

p = next;

}

start = prev;

}

}//End of reverse()

The following example shows all the steps of reversing a single linked list:

![A step-by-step diagram with nodes and arrows showing the reversal of a singly linked list, including updates to start, prev, next, and p pointers through each iteration until the list is reversed. ](images/Figure_3.017.png)

Figure 3.17 Steps of reversing a single linked list

## 3.2 Doubly Linked List

The linked list that we have studied contained only one link; this is why these lists are called single linked lists or one way lists. We could move only in one direction because each node has the reference to the next node only. Suppose we are in the middle of a linked list, and we want the reference to the previous node. Then, we have no way of doing this except repeating the traversal from the starting node. To overcome this drawback of single linked list, we have another data structure called the doubly linked list or two-way list, in which each node has two references. One of these references refers to the next node and the other refers to the previous node. Here is the class Node for doubly linked list:

class Node

{

public int info;

public Node prev;

public Node next;

public Node(int data)

{

info = data;

prev = null;

next = null;

}

}//End of class Node

Here, prev is a reference that will refer to the previous node and next will refer to the next node in the list. So, we can move in both directions at any time. The next reference of last node and prev reference of first node are null.

![Diagram of a doubly linked list showing nodes with three fields: information, next node reference, and previous node reference, with arrows indicating navigation between nodes. ](images/Figure_3.018.png)

Figure 3.18 Doubly linked list

The basic logic for all operations is the same as in single linked list, but here, we have to do a little extra work because there is one more reference that has to be updated each time. Here is the class for doubly linked list:

class DoublyLinkedList

{

private Node start;

//Methods

..........

..........

}//End of class DoublyLinkedList

The start will refer to the first node of list once nodes of doubly linked lists are created. It will be initialized to null in constructor, during the creation of DoublyLinkedList object.

The constructor and method isEmpty() will be the same as SingleLinkedList.

We will discuss the following operations on a doubly linked list:

*   Traversal of a doubly linked list
*   Searching an element
*   Insertion of an element
*   Deletion of an element
*   Creation of a doubly linked list
*   Reversal of a doubly linked list

The main() method is available in another class DoublyLinkedListDemo and given next. The code of methods of class DoublyLinkedList are given with the explanation of operations.

//DoublyLinkedList.java : Program of Doubly linked list.

class DoublyLinkedListDemo

{

public static void main(String[] args)

{

DoublyLinkedList list1 = new DoublyLinkedList();

//Create the List

list1.insertAtBeginning(10);

list1.insertAtEnd(30);

list1.insertAfter(50,30);

list1.insertAtPosition(20,2);

list1.insertBefore(40,50);

System.out.println(“List1 Items after insertion :”);

list1.display();

System.out.println(“Total items : “ + list1.size());

System.out.println(“find(40) = “ + list1.find(40));

DoublyLinkedList list2 = new DoublyLinkedList(list1);

System.out.println(“List2 Items after using copy constructor :”);

list2.display();

list1.deleteAtBeginning();

list1.deleteAtEnd();

list1.deleteNode(30);

list1.deleteAtPosition(2);

System.out.println(“List1 Items after deletion :”);

list1.display();

list2.reverse();

System.out.println(“List2 Items after reverse :”);

list2.display();

}//End of main()

}//End of class DoublyLinkedListDemo

### 3.2.1 Traversing a Doubly Linked List

Traversal of a doubly linked list is similar to traversal of a single linked list. We will use the reference next to traverse the list. Here is the method display():

public void display()

{

Node p;

if(!isEmpty())

{

p = start;

while(p != null)

{

System.out.println(p.info);

p = p.next;

}

}

else

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

}//End of display()

This is the method size() in which we traverse the list and count the number of nodes in it:

public int size()

{

Node p;

int count = 0;

p = start;

while(p != null)

{

count++;

p = p.next;

}

return count;

}//End of size()

### 3.2.2 Searching an Element in a Doubly Linked List

Searching an element in a doubly linked list is similar to searching for it in a single linked list. Here is the method find():

public int find(int nodeData)

{

Node p = start;

int position = 0;

while(p != null)

{

position++;

if(p.info == nodeData)

return position;

p = p.next;

}

return 0;

}//End of find()

### 3.2.3 Insertion in a Doubly Linked List

We will study all four cases of insertion in a doubly linked list:

*   Insertion at the beginning of the list
*   Insertion in an empty list
*   Insertion at the end of the list
*   Insertion in between the nodes

#### 3.2.3.1 Insertion at the Beginning of the List

![Diagram showing a linked list before and after insertion: Before insertion, Node P is in the list. After insertion, a new Node T is inserted after Node P, updating the pointers to include Node T. ](images/Figure_3.019.png)

Figure 3.19 Insertion at the beginning of the list

Node T has become the first node, so its prev should be null, which is done in constructor while creating the new node temp.

The next part of node T should refer to node P, and the reference to node P is in start, so we should write:

temp.next = start;

Node T is inserted before node P, so the prev part of the node P should now refer to node T:

start.prev = temp;

Now, node T has become the first node, so start should refer to it:

start = temp;

public void insertAtBeginning(int data)

{

Node temp;

temp = new Node(data);

if(!isEmpty())

{

temp.next = start;

start.prev = temp;

}

start = temp;

}//End of insertAtBeginning()

#### 3.2.3.2 Insertion in an Empty List

![Diagram showing two stages: Before insertion, start points to null. After insertion, start points to a new node labeled Node T, indicating a node was added to an empty linked list. ](images/Figure_3.020.png)

Figure 3.20 Insertion in an empty list

Node T is the first node, so its prev part should be null, and it is also the last node, so its next part should also be null. This is done in constructor while creating a new node temp. Node T is the first node so start should refer to it.

start = temp;

This case is taken care of in the previous case (3.2.3.1) where we are checking if the list is not empty, then only

temp.next refers to the next node and the next node prev refers to temp.

#### 3.2.3.3 Insertion at the End of the List

![Two diagrams show a linked list before and after insertion. Before: start points to a list ending at Node P. After: a new Node T is inserted after Node P, with arrows showing updated pointers. ](images/Figure_3.021.png)

Figure 3.21 Insertion at the end of the list

Let us suppose p is a reference referring to the node P, which is the last node of the list.

Node T becomes the last node, so its next should be null, which is already assigned with null, while creating the node temp.

The next part of node P should refer to node T:

p.next = temp;

The prev part of node T should refer to node P:

temp.prev = p;

Getting the reference p referring to the last node P, is similar to a single linked list:

p = start;

while(p.next != null)

p = p.next;

The following method insertAtEnd() inserts a node at the end of the list:

public void insertAtEnd(int data)

{

Node p, temp;

temp = new Node(data);

if(isEmpty())

start = temp;

else

{

p = start;

while (p.next != null)

p = p.next;

p.next = temp;

temp.prev = p;

}

}//End of insertAtEnd()

#### 3.2.3.4 Insertion in Between the Nodes

![Diagram of a linked list: left shows the list before insertion with nodes P and Q; right shows the list after inserting a new node T between nodes P and Q. ](images/Figure_3.022.png)

Figure 3.22 Insertion in between the nodes

Suppose references p and q refer to nodes P and Q, respectively.

Node P is before node T, so prev of node T should refer to node P:

temp.prev = p;

Node Q is after node T, so next part of node T should refer to node Q:

temp.next = q;

Node T is before node Q, so prev part of node Q should refer to node T:

q.prev = temp;

Node T is after node P, so next part of node P should refer to node T:

p.next = temp;

Now we will see three cases of insertion in between the nodes:

*   Insertion after a node
*   Insertion before a node
*   Insertion at a given position

##### 3.2.3.4.1 Insertion After a Node

In this case, we are given a value and the new node is to be inserted after the node containing this value. Suppose node P contains this value. Thus, we have to add a new node after node P. As in single linked list, here also we can traverse the list and find a reference p referring to node P. Now, in the four insertion statements, we can replace q by p.next.

temp.prev = p; -> temp.prev = p;

temp.next = q; -> temp.next = p.next;

q.prev = temp; -> p.next.prev = temp;

p.next = temp; -> p.next = temp;

Note that p.next should be changed at the end because we are using it in previous statements.

In single linked list, we had seen that the case of inserting after the last node was handled automatically. But here, when we insert after the last node, the third statement (p.next.prev = temp;)will create problems. The reference p refers to the last node, so its next is null. Hence, the term p.next.prev is meaningless here. To avoid this problem, we can put a check like this:

if(p.next != null)

p.next.prev = temp;

Here is the method insertAfter():

public void insertAfter(int data, int nodeData)

{

Node p, temp;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

p = start;

while(p != null)

{

if(p.info == nodeData)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.prev = p;

temp.next = p.next;

if(p.next != null)

p.next.prev = temp; //p refers to last node

p.next = temp;

break;

}

p = p.next;

}

if(p == null)

System.out.println(“Item “ + nodeData + “ is not in the list”);

}//End of else

}//End of insertAfter()

##### 3.2.3.4.2 Insertion Before a Node

In this case, we are given a value and the new node is to be inserted before the node containing this value. Suppose we have to insert the new node before node Q. We will traverse the list and find a reference q referring to node Q. In a single linked list, we had to find the reference to the predecessor, but here, there is no need to do so because we can get the reference to the predecessor by q.prev. So, just replace p by q.prev in the four insertion statements:

temp.prev = p;->temp.prev = q.prev;

temp.next = q;->temp.next = q;

q.prev = temp;->q.prev = temp;

p.next = temp;->q.prev.next = temp;

q.prev should be changed at the end because it is used in other statements. Thus, the third statement should be the last one.

temp.prev = q.prev;

temp.next = q;

q.prev.next = temp;

q.prev = temp;

As in a single linked list, here also, we will have to handle the case of insertion before the first node separately. Here is the method insertBefore(). In the code, we are using p instead of q:

public void insertBefore(int data, int nodeData)

{

Node p, temp;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else if(start.info == nodeData) //nodeData is in first node

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.next = start;

start.prev = temp;

start = temp;

}

else

{

p = start.next;

while(p != null)

{

if(p.info == nodeData)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.prev = p.prev;

temp.next = p;

p.prev.next = temp;

p.prev = temp;

break;

}

p = p.next;

}

if(p == null)

System.out.println(“Item “ + nodeData + “ is not in the List”);

}//End of else

}//End of insertBefore()

##### 3.2.3.4.3 Insertion at a Given Position

In this case, we have to insert the new node at a given position. We have to get the reference p to (position-1)th node (suppose it is node P). Then insert the node. As in a single linked list, insertion at the first position is handled separately. Here is the method insertAtPosition():

public void insertAtPosition(int data, int position)

{

Node temp, p;

if(position == 1)

{

temp = new Node(data);

if(!isEmpty())

{

temp.next = start;

start.prev = temp;

}

start = temp;

}

else

{

p = start;

int index = 1;

//Find a reference to (position-1)th node

while(p != null && index < position-1)

{

p = p.next;

index++;

}

if(p!=null && position>0)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.prev = p;

temp.next = p.next;

if(p.next != null) //p refers to last node

p.next.prev = temp;

p.next = temp;

}

else

System.out.println(“Item cannot be inserted at position : “ + position);

}//End of else

}//End of insertAtPosition()

### 3.2.4 Creation of List

A doubly linked list can be created using the insertion operations. First time, we will have to insert into an empty list, and then we will keep inserting nodes at the end of the list or insert at the beginning of the list or using any other insertion operation.

//Create the List

DoublyLinkedList list = new DoublyLinkedList();

list.insertAtEnd(10);

list.insertAtEnd(20);

list.insertAtEnd(30);

list.insertAtEnd(40);

list.insertAtEnd(50);

### 3.2.5 Deletion from a Doubly Linked List

As in a single linked list, here also, the node is removed by rearranging the references. Let us study the four cases of deletion:

*   Deletion of the first node
*   Deletion of the only node
*   Deletion in between the nodes
*   Deletion at the end

#### 3.2.5.1 Deletion of the First Node

![Two diagrams: Before deletion shows a linked list with nodes T and P; After deletion shows node P removed and node T linked directly to the next node, bypassing P. ](images/Figure_3.023.png)

Figure 3.23 Deletion of the first node

start will be updated to refer to node P:

start = start.next;

Now, node P is the first node, so its prev part should contain null.

start.prev = null;

Here is the method deleteAtBeginning():

public void deleteAtBeginning()

{

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

if(start.next == null) //If list has only 1 node

start = null;

else

{

start = start.next;

start.prev = null;

}

}

}//End of deleteAtBeginning()

#### 3.2.5.2 Deletion of the Only Node

![Diagram showing a linked list before and after deletion: Before deletion, the list points to Node T; after deletion, the lists start points to null. ](images/Figure_3.024.png)

Figure 3.24 Deletion of the only node

The statement for deletion will be:

start = null;

This case is taken care of in the previous case (3.2.5.1), where we check if the list has only one node, and then null is assigned to start.

#### 3.2.5.3 Deletion in Between the Nodes

![Diagram showing a singly linked list before and after deletion: Before deletion‚Äînodes P, T, and Q are connected in sequence. After deletion‚Äînode T is isolated, and node P points directly to node Q, bypassing node T. ](images/Figure_3.025.png)

Figure 3.25 Deletion in between the nodes

Suppose, we have to delete node T, and let references p, temp and q refer to nodes P, T and Q, respectively.

The two statements for deleting node T can be written as:

p.next = q;

q.prev = p;

The reference to q is in temp.next so we can replace q by temp.next.

p.next = temp.next;

temp.next.prev = p;

The reference to p is stored in temp.prev, so we can replace p by temp.prev.

temp.prev.next = temp.next;

temp.next.prev = temp.prev;

Thus, we need only a reference to the node T to delete it.

Now, we will see two cases of deletion in between the nodes:

*   Delete a node specified with value
*   Deletion of a node at a given position

##### 3.2.5.3.1 Delete a Node with Specified Value

In this case, we have to find the node with a specified value. The value is in node T, and we need reference p refering to node T. Thus, our condition for searching will be if(p.info == nodeData). Here, nodeData is the value in the node to be deleted.

The method deleteNode() deletes the node with a specified value.

public void deleteNode(int nodeData)

{

Node p;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

p = start;

while(p.next != null)

{

if(p.info == nodeData)

break;

p = p.next;

}

if(p.info == nodeData)

{

if(p.next == null)

{

if(p.prev == null) //First and only node

start = null;

else

p.prev.next = null; //Last node

}

else

{

if(p.prev == null) //First node

{

p.next.prev = null;

start = p.next;

}

else //Node in between

{

p.prev.next = p.next;

p.next.prev = p.prev;

}

}

}//End of if

else

System.out.println(nodeData + “ not found in list”);

}//End of else

}//End of deleteNode()

##### 3.2.5.3.2 Deletion of a Node at a Given Position

In this case, we have to delete the node at a given position. The deletion statements are the same as explained. We have to get the reference p refering to the node at the specified position.

The method deleteAtPosition() deletes the node at a given position:

public void deleteAtPosition(int position)

{

Node p;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

p = start;

int index = 1;

while(p.next != null)

{

if(index == position)

break;

index++;

p = p.next;

}

if(position == 1)

{

if(p.next == null) //First node of only node in list

start = null;

else //First node of more than one node in list

{

p.next.prev = null;

start = p.next;

}

}

else if(index == position)

{

if(p.next == null)

p.prev.next = null;

else

{

p.next.prev = p.prev;

p.prev.next = p.next;

}

}

else

System.out.println(“Node cannot be deleted at position : “ + position);

}//End of else

}//End of deleteAtPosition()

#### 3.2.5.4 Deletion at the End of the List

Suppose node T is to be deleted, and reference p refers to node T. The reference referring to node P is stored in prev of node T. The deletion can be performed by writing the following statement:

p.prev.next = null;

![Diagram showing two linked lists: Before deletion, nodes are ordered with arrows from start to node P to node T. After deletion, node T is removed, and node P follows directly after the deleted nodes previous position. ](images/Figure_3.026.png)

Figure 3.26 Deletion at the end of the list

This is the method deleteAtEnd():

public void deleteAtEnd()

{

Node p;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

p = start;

while(p.next != null)

p = p.next;

if(p.prev != null)

p.prev.next = null;

else

start = null;

}

}//End of deleteAtEnd()

### 3.2.6 Copy Constructor

Copy constructor in a doubly linked list is similar as provided in a single linked list.

Here is the copy constructor of a doubly linked list:

public DoublyLinkedList(DoublyLinkedList list)

{

if(list.start == null)

start = null;

else

{

Node p1, p2, previous;

p1 = list.start;

p2 = start = new Node(p1.info);

previous = null;

p1 = p1.next;

while(p1 != null)

{

p2.next = new Node(p1.info);

p2.prev = previous;

previous = p2;

p2 = p2.next;

p1 = p1.next;

}

p2.prev = previous;

}

}//End of copy constructor

### 3.2.7 Reversing a Doubly Linked List

Let us take a doubly linked list and see what changes need to be made for its reversal. The following figure shows a doubly linked list and the reversed linked list:

![Two diagrams of linked lists: the left shows a singly linked list from start to Node A, B, C, and D; the right shows a doubly linked list with arrows pointing forward and backward between nodes. ](images/Figure_3.027.png)

Figure 3.27 Reversing a doubly linked list

In the reversed list-

(i) start refers to Node D

(ii) Node D is the first node so its prev is null

(iii) Node A is the last node so its next is null

(iv) next of D refers to C, next of C refers to B and next of B refers to A

(v) prev of A refers to B, prev of B refers to C, prev of C refers to D

For making the method of reversal of a doubly linked list, we will need only two references:

public void reverse()

{

Node p, temp;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

p = start;

while(p.next != null)

{

temp = p.next;

p.next = p.prev;

p.prev = temp;

p = temp;

}

p.next = p.prev;

p.prev = null;

start = p;

}

}//End of reverse()

In a doubly linked list, we have an extra reference, which consumes extra space, and the maintenance of this reference makes operations lengthy and time-consuming. So, doubly linked lists are beneficial only when we frequently need the predecessor of a node.

## 3.3 Circular Linked List

In a single linked list, for accessing any node of linked list we start traversing from first node. If we are at any node in the middle of the list, then it is not possible to access nodes that precede the given node. This problem can be solved by slightly altering the structure of a single linked list. In a single linked list, the link part of the last node is null. If we utilize this link to refer to the first node, then we can have some advantages. The structure thus formed is called a circular linked list. The following figure shows a circular linked list:

![A horizontal sequence of boxes contains the numbers 3, 9, 1, 5, 8, and 6\. Arrows connect each box from left to right, forming a row, with a final arrow looping from the last to the first box. ](images/Figure_3.028.png)

Figure 3.28 Circular linked list

Each node has a successor, and all the nodes form a ring. Now, we can access any node of the linked list without going back. We can start traversal again from the first node because the list is in the form of a circle, and we can go from the last node to the first node.

We take an external reference that refers to the last node of the list. If we have a reference last referring to the last node, then last.link will refer to the first node.

![A diagram of a singly linked list with four nodes. Node P points to the first node, and Node Z points to the last node, with an arrow labeled last indicating the end of the list. ](images/Figure_3.029.png)

Figure 3.29 Circular list with a reference referring to last node

In figure 3.29, the reference last refers to node Z and last.link refers to node P. Let us see why we have taken a reference that refers to the last node instead of first node. Suppose, we take a reference start referring to the first node of circular linked list. Take the case of an insertion of a node in the beginning.

![Diagram showing two linked lists. Left: start points to Node P, which links to two more nodes, ending at Node Z. Right: start points to Node T, which links to Node P, then two more nodes, ending at Node Z. ](images/Figure_3.030.png)

Figure 3.30 Circular list with a reference referring to first node

For insertion of node T in the beginning, we need the reference to node Z, because we have to change the link of node Z and make it refer to node T. Thus, we will have to traverse the whole list. For insertion at the end, it is obvious that the whole list has to be traversed. If instead of reference start, we take a reference to the last node. Then in both the cases, there will not be any need to traverse the whole list. So, insertion in the beginning or at the end takes constant time irrespective of the length of the list.

If the circular list is empty, the reference last is null, and if the list contains only one element, then the link of last refers to last.

The class Node is same as single linked list:

class Node

{

public int info;

public Node link;

public Node(int data)

{

info = data;

link = null;

}

}//End of class Node

The basic logic for all operations is the same as in single linked list, but here we have to make sure that after completing any operation, the link of last node refers to the first. Here is the class CircularLinkedList for circular linked list:

class CircularLinkedList

{

private Node last;

//Methods

..........

..........

}//End of class CircularLinkedList

The reference last will refer to the last node of list and the link of the last node will refer to first node. It will be initialized to null in constructor, during the creation of CircularLinkedList object.

This is the constructor of class CircularLinkedList:

public CircularLinkedList()

{

last = null;

}//End of CircularLinkedList()

The following method isEmpty() returns true if list is empty, otherwise false.

public boolean isEmpty()

{

return (last == null);

}//End of isEmpty()

We will discuss the following operations on a circular linked list:

*   Traversal of a circular linked list
*   Insertion of an element
*   Deletion of an element
*   Creation of a circular linked list
*   Reversal of a circular linked list

The main() method is available in another class CircularLinkedListDemo and given next. The code of methods of class CircularLinkedList are given with the explanation of operations.

//CircularLinkedList.java : Program of Circular linked list.

class CircularLinkedListDemo

{

public static void main(String[] args)

{

CircularLinkedList list1 = new CircularLinkedList();

//Create the List

list1.insertAtBeginning(10);

list1.insertAtEnd(30);

list1.insertAfter(50,30);

list1.insertAtPosition(20,2);

list1.insertBefore(40,50);

System.out.println(“List1 Items after insertion :”);

list1.display();

CircularLinkedList list2 = new CircularLinkedList(list1);

System.out.println(“List2 Items after using copy constructor :”);

list2.display();

list1.deleteAtBeginning();

list1.deleteAtEnd();

list1.deleteNode(30);

list1.deleteAtPosition(2);

System.out.println(“List1 Items after deletion :”);

list1.display();

list2.reverse();

System.out.println(“List2 Items after reverse :”);

list2.display();

CircularLinkedList list4 = new CircularLinkedList();

CircularLinkedList list5 = new CircularLinkedList();

list4.insertAtEnd(10);

list4.insertAtEnd(20);

list4.insertAtEnd(30);

list4.insertAtEnd(40);

list4.insertAtEnd(50);

System.out.println(“List4 Items :”);

list4.display();

list5.insertAtEnd(5);

list5.insertAtEnd(15);

list5.insertAtEnd(25);

list5.insertAtEnd(35);

list5.insertAtEnd(45);

System.out.println(“List5 Items :”);

list5.display();

list4.concatenate(list5);

System.out.println(“List4 Items after concatenation :”);

list4.display();

}//End of main()

}//End of class CircularLinkedListDemo

### 3.3.1 Traversal of a Circular Linked List

First of all, we will check if the list is empty. After that, we will take a reference p and make it refer to the first node.

p = last.link;

The link of last node does not contain null, but contains the reference to the first node, so here the terminating condition of our loop becomes (p != last.link).

Here is the method display():

public void display()

{

Node p;

if(!isEmpty())

{

p = last.link;

do

{

System.out.println(p.info);

p = p.link;

}while(p != last.link);

}

else

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

}//End of display()

We have used a do-while loop because if we take a while loop, then the terminating condition will be satisfied in the first time itself and the loop will not execute at all.

### 3.3.2 Insertion in a Circular Linked List

We will study all the four cases of insertion in a circular linked list:

*   Insertion at the beginning of the list
*   Insertion in an empty list
*   Insertion at the end of the list
*   Insertion in between the nodes

#### 3.3.2.1 Insertion at the Beginning of the List

![Two diagrams compare a circular linked list before and after inserting Node Z after Node P. Both show nodes connected in a loop, with the last pointer updated to Node Z after insertion. ](images/Figure_3.031.png)

Figure 3.31 Insertion at the beginning of the list

Before insertion, P is the first node so last.link refers to node P.

After insertion, the link of node T should refer to node P and reference to node P is in the last.link.

temp.link = last.link;

The link of the last node should refer to node T:

last.link = temp;

public void insertAtBeginning(int data)

{

Node temp;

temp = new Node(data);

if(isEmpty())

{

last = temp;

last.link = temp;

}

else

{

temp.link = last.link;

last.link = temp;

}

}//End of insertAtBeginning()

#### 3.3.2.2 Insertion in an Empty List

![Two diagrams: Left‚ÄîA single box labeled last with value null and caption Before insertion. Right‚ÄîA node labeled Node T added, with last pointing to it and caption After insertion. ](images/Figure_3.032.png)

Figure 3.32 Insertion in an empty list

After insertion, T is the last node so reference last refers to node T.

last = temp;

We know that last.link always refers to the first node. Here, T is the first node so last.link  refers to node T (or last).

last.link = temp;

This case is taken care in the previous case (3.3.2.1) where we are checking if the list is empty, then only last and last.link both refers to new inserted node temp.

#### 3.3.2.3 Insertion at the End of the List

![Diagram showing a linked list before and after insertion: Before, last points to Node P; after insertion, a new Node T is added after Node P, and last now points to Node T. ](images/Figure_3.033.png)

Figure 3.33 Insertion at the end of the list

Before insertion, last refers to node P and last.link refers to node A.

After insertion, link of T should refer to node A. The reference last.link refers to node A:

temp.link = last.link;

Link of node P should refer to node T:

last.link = temp;

last should refer to node T:

last = temp;

The order of the above three statements is important.

public void insertAtEnd(int data)

{

Node temp;

temp = new Node(data);

if(isEmpty())

{

last = temp;

last.link = temp;

}

else

{

temp.link = last.link;

last.link = temp;

last = temp;

}

}//End of insertAtEnd()

#### 3.3.2.4 Insertion in Between the Nodes

The logic for insertion in between the nodes is the same as in single linked list. If the insertion is done after the last node, then the reference last should be updated.

We have three cases of insertion in between the nodes:

*   Insertion after a node
*   Insertion before a node
*   Insertion at a given position

##### 3.3.2.4.1 Insertion After a Node

Here is the method insertAfter() for insertion after a node:

public void insertAfter(int data, int nodeData)

{

Node p, temp;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

p = last.link;

do

{

if(p.info == nodeData)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = p.link;

p.link = temp;

if(p == last)

last = temp;

break;

}

p = p.link;

}while(p != last.link);

if(p == last.link)

System.out.println(“Item “ + nodeData + “ is not in the list”);

}//End of else

}//End of insertAfter()

##### 3.3.2.4.2 Insertion Before a Node

Here is the method insertBefore() for insertion before a node:

public void insertBefore(int data, int nodeData)

{

Node p, temp;

p = last;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else if(p.link.info == nodeData) //nodeData is in first node

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = p.link;

p.link = temp;

}

else

{

p = last.link;

do

{

if(p.link.info == nodeData)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = p.link;

p.link = temp;

break;

}

p = p.link;

}while(p != last.link);

if(p == last.link)

System.out.println(“Item “ + nodeData + “ is not in the list”);

}//End of else

}//End of insertBefore()

##### 3.3.2.4.3 Insertion at a Given Position

Here is the method insertAtPosition() for insertion at a given position:

public void insertAtPosition(int data, int position)

{

Node p, temp;

p = last;

if(isEmpty())

{

if(position == 1)

{

temp = new Node(data);

last = temp;

last.link = temp;

}

else

System.out.println(“Item cannot be inserted at position : “ + position);

}

else if(position == 1)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = last.link;

last.link = temp;

}

else

{

p = last.link;

int index = 1;

do

{

if(index == position-1)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = p.link;

p.link = temp;

if(p == last)

last = temp;

p = p.link;

break;

}

index++;

p = p.link;

}while(p != last.link);

if(p == last.link)

System.out.println(“Item cannot be inserted at position : “ + position);

}//End of else

}//End of insertAtPosition()

### 3.3.3 Creation of Circular Linked List

A list can be created using insertion operations similar to those of single linked list:

//Create the List

CircularLinkedList list = new CircularLinkedList();

list.insertAtEnd(10);

list.insertAtEnd(20);

list.insertAtEnd(30);

list.insertAtEnd(40);

list.insertAtEnd(50);

### 3.3.4 Deletion in Circular Linked List

Deletion in a circular linked list is similar to deletion in a single linked list. There can be four cases while deleting an element from a circular linked list:

*   Deletion of the first node
*   Deletion of the only node
*   Deletion in between the nodes
*   Deletion at the end of the list

#### 3.3.4.1 Deletion of the First Node

Before deletion, last refers to node Z and last.link refers to node T.

After deletion, the link of node Z should refer to node A. Thus, last.link should refer to node A. The reference to node A is in the link of node T.

last.link = temp.link;

![Two diagrams of a circular linked list: left shows three nodes (T, A, Z) before deletion, with ‚Äòlast‚Äô pointing to Z; right shows two nodes (A, Z) after deletion, with ‚Äòlast‚Äô pointing to Z. ](images/Figure_3.034.png)

Figure 3.34 Deletion of the first node

public void deleteAtBeginning()

{

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else if(last.link == last) //List has only one node

last = null;

else

last.link = last.link.link;

}//End of deleteAtBeginning()

#### 3.3.4.2 Deletion of the Only Node

If there is only one element in the list, then we assign null value to the reference last because after deletion there will be no node in the list.

![Diagram showing a linked list: Before deletion, ‚Äòlast‚Äô points to Node T; after deletion, ‚Äòlast‚Äô points to null and Node T is removed. ](images/Figure_3.035.png)

Figure 3.35 Deletion of the only node

There will be only one node in the list, if the link of last node refers to itself. After deletion the list will become empty, and so null is assigned to last.

last = null;

This case is taken care of in the previous case (3.3.4.1), where we are checking if the list has only one node, then node is deleted by assigning null to last.

#### 3.3.4.3 Deletion in Between the Nodes

Deletion in between is the same, as in the case of a single linked list. We have two cases of deletion in between the nodes:

*   Delete a node specified with value
*   Deletion of a node at a given position

##### 3.3.4.3.1 Delete a Node Specified with Value

Here is the method deleteNode() to delete a node specified with value:

public void deleteNode(int nodeData)

{

Node p;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else if(last.link.info == nodeData) //Deletion of first node

{

if(last.link == last) //List has only one node

last = null;

else

last.link = last.link.link;

}

else //Deletion in between or at the end

{

p = last.link;

while(p.link != last.link)

{

if(p.link.info == nodeData)

break;

p = p.link;

}

if(p.link == last.link)

System.out.println(nodeData + “ not found in list”);

else

{

if(p.link == last)

last = p;

p.link = p.link.link;

}

}//End of else

}//End of deleteNode()

##### 3.3.4.3.2 Deletion of a Node at a Given Position

Here is the method deleteAtPosition() to delete a node at a given position:

public void deleteAtPosition(int position)

{

Node p;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else if(position == 1) //Deletion of first node

{

if(last.link == last) //List has only one node

last = null;

else

last.link = last.link.link;

}

else //Deletion in between or at the end

{

p = last.link;

int index = 1;

while(p.link != last.link)

{

if(index == position-1)

break;

index++;

p = p.link;

}

if(p.link == last.link)

System.out.println(“Node cannot be deleted at position : “ + position);

else

{

if(p.link == last)

last = p;

p.link = p.link.link;

}

}//End of else

}//End of deleteAtPosition()

#### 3.3.4.4 Deletion at the End of the List

![Two diagrams of linked lists: before deletion, nodes A, P, and T are linked, with last pointing to T; after deletion, only nodes A and P remain, with last now pointing to P. ](images/Figure_3.036.png)

Figure 3.36 Deletion at the end of the list

Before deletion, last refers to node T and last.link refers to node A, p is a reference to node P. After deletion, the link of node P should refer to node A. The reference to node A is in the last.link.

p.link = last.link;

Now, P is the last node, so last should refer to node P.

last = p;

public void deleteAtEnd()

{

Node p;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else if(last.link == last) //List has only one node

{

last = null;

}

else

{

p = last.link;

while(p.link != last)

p = p.link;

p.link = last.link;

last = p;

}

}//End of deleteAtEnd()

### 3.3.5 Copy Constructor

Copy constructor in a circular linked list is similar to that in a single linked list.

Here is the copy constructor of a circular linked list:

public CircularLinkedList(CircularLinkedList list)

{

if(list.last == null)

last = null;

else

{

Node p1, p2;

p1 = list.last.link;

p2 = last = new Node(p1.info);

last.link = last;

p1 = p1.link;

while(p1 != list.last.link)

{

Node temp = new Node(p1.info);

temp.link = p2.link;

p2.link = temp;

p2 = p2.link;

last = p2;

p1 = p1.link;

}

}//End of else

}//End of copy constructor

### 3.3.6 Reversing a Circular Linked List

Here is the method reverse() to reverse a circular linked list:

public void reverse()

{

Node prev, p, next;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

p = last.link;

prev = last;

while(p.link != last.link)

{

next = p.link;

p.link = prev;

prev = p;

p = next;

}

last = p.link;

last.link = p;

p.link = prev;

}

}//End of reverse()

We have studied circular lists which are singly linked. Doubly linked lists can also be made circular. In this case, the reference next of last node refers to the first node, and the reference prev of first node refers to the last node.

![A block diagram showing four rectangular blocks connected in a loop by arrows, with an additional arrow pointing into the first block from above and an arrow leaving the last block from above. ](images/Figure_3.037.png)

Figure 3.37 Circular doubly linked list

## 3.4 Linked List with Header Node

Header node is a dummy node that is present at the beginning of the list and its link part refers to the first actual node of the list. The info part of this node may be empty or can be used to contain useful information about the list, such as count of elements currently present in the list. Figure 3.38 (a) shows a single linked list with 4 actual nodes and a header node, and figure 3.38 (b) shows an empty list with a header node.

![Diagram showing two singly linked lists: (a) has four connected nodes with the first node shaded, labeled List with 4 nodes; (b) is an empty list with head pointing to a shaded box, labeled Empty list. ](images/Figure_3.038.png)

Figure 3.38 Single linked list with header node

The reference head refers to the header node and head.link refers to the first true node of the list. If there is no node in the list, then head.link will be null.

The header node is never removed; it exists even if the list is empty. So, it is created while creating object of class SingleLinkedListH.

The use of header nodes makes the program simple and faster. Since, the list is never empty because the header node is always there, we can avoid some special cases of empty list and that of insertion and deletion in the beginning. For example, in the method deleteNode() and insertBefore() that we had written for single linked list, we can drop the first two cases if we take a header node in our list.

The following program performs operations on a single linked list with the header node. The logic of all operations is similar to that of single linked list without the header, but some cases have been removed.

//SingleLinkedListH.java : Program of single linked list with header node.

class Node

{

public int info;

public Node link;

public Node(int data)

{

info = data;

link = null;

}

}//End of class Node

class SingleLinkedListH

{

private Node head;

public SingleLinkedListH()

{

head = new Node(0);

}//End of SingleLinkedListH()

public SingleLinkedListH(SingleLinkedListH list)

{

Node p1, p2;

p1 = list.head;

p2 = head = new Node(p1.info);

p1 = p1.link;

while(p1 != null)

{

p2.link = new Node(p1.info);

p2 = p2.link;

p1 = p1.link;

}

}//End of copy constructor

public boolean isEmpty()

{

return (head.link == null);

}//End of isEmpty()

public void display()

{

Node p;

if(!isEmpty())

{

p = head.link;

while(p != null)

{

System.out.println(p.info);

p = p.link;

}

}

else

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

}//End of display()

public void insertAtBeginning(int data)

{

Node temp;

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = head.link;

head.link = temp;

}//End of insertAtBeginning()

public void insertAtEnd(int data)

{

Node p, temp;

temp = new Node(data);

p = head;

while(p.link != null)

p = p.link;

p.link = temp;

}//End of insertAtEnd()

public void insertBefore(int data, int nodeData)

{

Node p, temp;

p = head;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

//Find the reference to predecessor of node containing nodeData

while(p.link != null)

{

if(p.link.info == nodeData)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = p.link;

p.link = temp;

break;

}

p = p.link;

}

if(p.link == null)

System.out.println(“Item “ + nodeData + “ is not in the List”);

}//End of else

}//End of insertBefore()

public void insertAfter(int data, int nodeData)

{

Node p, temp;

p = head.link;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

while(p != null)

{

if(p.info == nodeData)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = p.link;

p.link = temp;

break;

}

p = p.link;

}

if(p == null)

System.out.println(“Item “ + nodeData + “ is not in the list”);

}//End of else

}//End of insertAfter()

public void insertAtPosition(int data, int position)

{

Node p, temp;

if(position == 1)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = head.link;

head.link = temp;

}

else

{

p = head.link;

int index = 1;

//Find the reference to (position-1)th node

while(p!=null && index < position-1)

{

p = p.link;

index++;

}

if(p!=null && position>0)

{

temp = new Node(data);

temp.link = p.link;

p.link = temp;

}

else

System.out.println(“Item cannot be inserted at position : “ + position);

}//End of else

}//End of insertAtPosition()

public void deleteAtBeginning()

{

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

head.link = head.link.link;

}//End of deleteAtBeginning()

public void deleteAtEnd()

{

Node p;

p = head;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

while(p.link.link != null)

p = p.link;

p.link = null;

}

}//End of deleteAtEnd()

public void deleteNode(int nodeData)

{

Node p;

p = head;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

while(p.link != null)

{

if(p.link.info == nodeData)

break;

p = p.link;

}

if(p.link == null)

System.out.println(nodeData + “ not found in list”);

else

p.link = p.link.link;

}//End of else

}//End of deleteNode()

public void deleteAtPosition(int position)

{

Node p;

p = head.link;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else if(position == 1)

head.link = p.link;

else

{

int index = 1;

while(p.link!=null && index < position-1)

{

p = p.link;

index++;

}

if(p.link!=null && position>0)

p.link = p.link.link;

else

System.out.println(“Node cannot be deleted at position : “ + position);

}//End of else

}//End of deleteAtPosition()

public void reverse()

{

Node prev, p, next;

if(isEmpty())

System.out.println(“List is empty”);

else

{

p = head.link;

prev = null;

while(p != null)

{

next = p.link;

p.link = prev;

prev = p;

p = next;

}

head.link = prev;

}

}//End of reverse()

}//End of class SingleLinkedListH

class SingleLinkedListHDemo

{

public static void main(String[] args)

{

SingleLinkedListH list1 = new SingleLinkedListH();

//Create the List

list1.insertAtBeginning(10);

list1.insertAtEnd(30);

list1.insertAfter(50,30);

list1.insertAtPosition(20,2);

list1.insertBefore(40,50);

System.out.println(“List1 Items after insertion :”);

list1.display();

SingleLinkedListH list2 = new SingleLinkedListH(list1);

System.out.println(“List2 Items after using copy constructor :”);

list2.display();

list1.deleteAtBeginning();

list1.deleteAtEnd();

list1.deleteNode(30);

list1.deleteAtPosition(2);

System.out.println(“List1 Items after deletion :”);

list1.display();

list2.reverse();

System.out.println(“List2 Items after reverse :”);

list2.display();

}//End of main()

}//End of class SingleLinkedListHDemo

The header node can be attached to circular linked lists and doubly linked lists also. The following figure shows a circular single linked list with header node:

![Two diagrams: one shows a circular linked list with three nodes labeled ‚ÄúList with 3 nodes‚Äù; the other shows a single head pointer pointing to an empty node labeled ‚ÄúEmpty list.‚Äù. ](images/Figure_3.039.png)

Figure 3.39 Circular single linked list with header

Here, the external reference refers to the header node rather than at the end.

The following figures show doubly linked list and doubly linked circular list with header nodes:

![Diagram showing two linked lists: one with three connected nodes labeled List with 3 nodes and the other with a single node pointing to nothing, labeled Empty list. Both have arrows labeled head. ](images/Figure_3.040.png)

Figure 3.40 Doubly linked list with header

![Diagram showing two linked lists: on the left, a circular doubly linked list with 3 nodes and a head pointer; on the right, an empty list with a head pointer and no nodes. ](images/Figure_3.041.png)

Figure 3.41 Doubly linked circular list with header

## 3.5 Sorted Linked List

In some applications, it is better if the elements in the list are kept in sorted order. For maintaining a list in sorted order, we have to insert the nodes in proper place. Let us take an ascending order linked list and insert some elements in it.

![A step-by-step diagram showing insertion of 29, 6, and 50 into a sorted linked list. Each step highlights the updated structure: Initial List (11‚Üí22‚Üí33), then 29 added, then 6 added at the start, then 50 at the end. ](images/Figure_3.042.png)

Figure 3.42 Insertion in a sorted linked list

When the element to be inserted is smaller than the first element, it will be inserted in the beginning. When the element to be inserted is greater than the last element, it will be inserted at the end. In other cases, the element will be inserted in the list at its proper place.

We will have a method insert() that will insert an element in the list, such that the ascending order is maintained. We have the same 4 cases as in other lists:

*   Insertion in the beginning
*   Insertion in an empty list
*   Insertion at the end
*   Insertion in between

Since, we have taken a single linked list, insertion in beginning and insertion in an empty list can be handled in the same way.

if(isEmpty() || data < start.info)

{

temp.link = start;

start = temp;

}

For insertion in between, we will traverse the list and find a reference to the node after which our new node should be inserted.

p = start;

while(p.link!=null && p.link.info < data)

p = p.link;

The new node has to be inserted after the node which is referred by reference p. The two lines of insertion are the same as in single linked list:

temp.link = p.link;

p.link = temp;

If the insertion is to be done at the end, then too, the above statements will work.

Other methods such as display(), size() etc., will remain the same. The method find() will be altered a little because here we can stop our search as soon as we find an element with value larger than the given element to be searched. The methods such as insertAtBeginning(), insertAtEnd(), insertBefore(), insertAfter(), insertAtPosition() do not make sense here because if we use these methods, then the sorted order of the list might get disturbed. The method insert() decides where the element has to be inserted and inserts it in the proper place. The process of deletion is the same as in single linked list but searching will be different.

//SortedLinkedList.java : Program of sorted linked list.

class Node

{

public int info;

public Node link;

public Node(int data)

{

info = data;

link = null;

}

}//End of class Node

class SortedLinkedList

{

private Node start;

public SortedLinkedList()

{

start = null;

}//End of SortedLinkedList()

public boolean isEmpty()

{

return (start == null);

}//End of isEmpty()

public void display()

{

Node p;

if(!isEmpty())

{

p = start;

while(p != null)

{
